say: You give it a cubic equation, $f(x) = 0$. It finds **all three roots**.
The key idea: once one root $a$ is known, $(x-a)$ divides the cubic exactly, and what is left is a quadratic you can already solve.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it on Paper 1, about one part most years, worth 10 or 15 marks: find one root by trial (or from an earlier part), divide it out, then solve the quadratic.

steps.title: Find one root by trial
steps.say: Try small whole numbers in $f(x)$. A root is a value that makes $f(x) = 0$.

lines.text: So $x = 3$ is a root, and $(x - 3)$ is a factor.

steps.title: Divide by the factor
steps.say: Divide the cubic by $(x - 3)$ using long division. Whatever is left is a quadratic.

lines.text: $2x^3 \div x = 2x^2$. Subtract $2x^2(x-3)$, bring down the next term, and repeat.
The remainder is $0$, so the division is exact.

steps.title: Factorise the quadratic
steps.say: Now solve $\hl{2}{2x^2 + 3x - 2} = 0$. Split the middle term: $3x = 4x - x$.

steps.title: Read off the three roots
steps.say: A product is zero when one factor is zero. Set each factor $(x-3)$, $(2x-1)$ and $(x+2)$ equal to $0$.

higher.tip: Finish the division and show that nothing is left over. A division completed with no remainder earns marks, and so does stating that there is no remainder.

sources.quote: No remainder in division may be stated

higher.tip: Write the quadratic you get after dividing. Finding the quotient in quadratic form earns High Partial Credit.
Do not just write down the three roots. Correct answers with no work earn only Low Partial Credit.
Trying values until one works is only the first step. Trials alone earn Low Partial Credit, so go on and divide.

say: You give it an expression with several terms. It gives back a shorter one with each kind of term **added up** once.
The key idea: only like terms combine, meaning the same letter to the same power. $7a$ and $3a$ combine; $7a$ and $4b$ do not.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level uses it as a step inside simplifying questions on Paper 1. In 2015 it sat inside Q3(a), a 15-mark part to simplify an expression.

steps.title: Group the like terms
steps.say: Put the terms with the same letter together. Each term keeps its sign.

lines.text: The sign in front of a term goes with it when it moves.

steps.title: Add each group
steps.say: Add the numbers in front of each letter. The letter stays the same.

ordinary.tip: Show the simplifying even if you are not sure of the answer. Some correct attempt at simplifying earns partial credit.

say: You give it an expression and a value for each letter. It gives back a **number**.
The key idea: put each value in place of its letter, in brackets, then do the arithmetic in the right order.

how.higher: Higher level uses it rarely: in 2015 Paper 2 Q9(c)(i) it was a 5-mark part that put $t=0$ into a height formula.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level uses it every year on Paper 1, often as the first part of a question (about 18 parts as the main skill): put a value into a function or formula and work out the number.

steps.title: Substitute the value
steps.say: Replace every $x$ with $\hl{1}{3}$. Put it in brackets.

steps.title: Work out the powers
steps.say: Powers come before multiplying. Work out $3^3$ and $3^2$ first, then multiply.

steps.title: Add and subtract
steps.say: Now work from left to right.

higher.tip: Write down the value you are substituting. Indicating $t = 0$ earns partial credit.
A correct value is accepted without working here, but writing the substitution protects you if the number is wrong.

ordinary.tip: Write the substitution out. Some correct substitution earns partial credit even if the arithmetic goes wrong.
A fully correct substitution, with the value in place of every letter, reaches High Partial Credit.
If the substitution gives fractions, work towards a single fraction. That earns partial credit.
A correct answer on its own can earn full credit, but showing the substitution protects you if you slip.

say: You give it a bracket with a number or letter outside it. It gives back the same expression **without the bracket**.
The key idea: the term outside multiplies every term inside, and its sign goes with it.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step inside bigger questions, for example in 2019 Paper 1 Q9(c)(i), a 5-mark part that builds an area formula.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level uses it often on Paper 1 as a step in simplifying, solving equations and building formulas; two parts test it as the main skill (2015 Q3(a) and 2016 Q8(d)(i)).

steps.title: Expand the second bracket
steps.say: Multiply every term in $(x - 6)$ by $-2$. The minus sign goes with the $2$.

lines.text: $-2 \times -6 = +12$. Two minus signs make a plus.

steps.title: Collect like terms
steps.say: Write both results together and add the $x$ terms and the numbers.

higher.tip: Build a formula from its pieces and write each piece down. The area of the rectangle and the area of the semi-circle each earn Low Partial Credit.

ordinary.tip: Show the bracket being multiplied out as its own step. Distributing the 3 is a marked step.
Multiply out every term. Multiplying out the equation correctly is a mark of its own.
Even one correctly multiplied term earns Low Partial Credit, so write each product out.
